v: In nineteen twelve, someone paid five hundred dollars for an empty lot in north Calgary.
That owner paid taxes on it for four decades. When it finally sold, in nineteen fifty-five, it went for four hundred.
How did Calgary get sold that far ahead of itself? This is Calgary Origins, episode three. Boom and bust.
In nineteen oh one, Calgary had only about four thousand people.
Ten years later, the census counted nearly forty-four thousand.
That's nearly ten times as many people, in a single decade.
What drove it? Farming, first of all. The opening of southern Alberta to cash crops brought rapid growth to Calgary.
Railways stretched out in all directions, and Calgary became the region's prime distributing centre.
By nineteen fourteen, prairie settlement had pushed far to the northwest, drawing migrants from many lands.
All those people needed places to live and work. So Calgary built.
In nineteen ten, the value of building permits was nearly five point six million dollars.
In nineteen eleven, almost thirteen million.
In nineteen twelve, more than twenty million dollars: a record.
The Grain Exchange, from nineteen ten, is remembered as Calgary's first skyscraper.
City Hall, one of the biggest building projects in town, went up between nineteen oh seven and nineteen eleven.
In nineteen twelve, the Lougheed Building was completed, with a fifteen-hundred-seat theatre inside: the Sherman Grand.
The same year, the Memorial Park Library opened: the first public library building in Alberta.
The Hudson's Bay Company store opened in nineteen thirteen, and the Canadian Pacific Railway was building a grand hotel, the Palliser, from nineteen eleven to nineteen fourteen.
Many of those buildings still stand downtown today.
Library, Bay or Palliser: which one have you been inside? Drop your thoughts below.
Some Calgary suburbs were sold before they were ever built, and at least one never was.
During the boom, speculators bought farmland outside the city limits and registered subdivision plans.
Agents advertised lots up to about eight kilometres from the central post office.
They asked between fifty and three hundred dollars a lot.
Heritage Calgary describes numerous dealers buying up land for resale all around the city.
The biggest name was Fred Lowes. Historian Max Foran calls him Calgary's most important real estate entrepreneur of the boom years.
He came to Calgary in nineteen oh two, and set up his own development firm in nineteen oh six.
His company had offices in Edmonton, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat, and even London, England.
In nineteen eleven, the Canadian Pacific Railway laid out South Mount Royal as an exclusive neighbourhood of single-family homes.
The northeast part of Upper Mount Royal drew a number of American-born entrepreneurs and speculators, and it became known as American Hill.
Far to the northwest, John Hextall registered subdivision plans for Bowness in nineteen eleven.
In Elbow Park, serious building began in nineteen eleven, near the height of the boom.
And in nineteen ten, the City annexed a vast area on all sides. Its western edge moved out to Thirty-seventh Street.
In the northwest, that line held until nineteen sixty-three. In the southwest, until nineteen fifty-four.
Then there was Lake View Heights. In May nineteen twelve, its ads promised: we do guarantee to complete by October first, nineteen thirteen.
It appears on a city map engraved in nineteen twelve. Heritage Calgary calls it an imaginary suburb, existing only on maps, never built.
Today, that land is a golf course.
Would you have bought a lot out on the open prairie? Yes or no? Drop your thoughts below.
By the end of nineteen thirteen, every one of downtown's four hundred real estate offices had shut.
How did a record year turn into that?
Alberta's land boom peaked in nineteen twelve, and went bust in nineteen thirteen.
Historian Paul Chastko points to events far away. The Balkan Wars disrupted Britain, and sharply cut British investment in Canada.
Chastko writes that this dealt a heavy blow to Calgary investors in construction and real estate.
Work on the great transcontinental railway projects was ending too, throwing thousands of labourers out of work.
In nineteen thirteen, the value of building permits fell to less than half of the year before.
The number of permits fell too, from three thousand, three hundred and forty-eight to two thousand and seventy-eight.
House prices began to fall.
By December nineteen thirteen, one in ten Calgarians was out of work: about two thousand tradesmen, and three thousand unskilled labourers.
Chastko writes that all four hundred real estate concerns in downtown Calgary sat closed and shuttered.
Then, in May nineteen fourteen, came a strange second wave. At Turner Valley, the Dingman well struck wet natural gas.
Oil fever swept Calgary. More than five hundred oil companies were started, most of them, says Alberta's energy history, ill-founded.
Many of the brokers were former real estate agents who had fallen on hard times when the housing boom collapsed.
Then, in August nineteen fourteen, the First World War began.
Interest in houses vanished, as thousands of Calgarians enlisted to serve overseas.
By the end of the war, all but twenty-one of those oil companies had failed, most without drilling a single well.
Boom or bubble: which word fits nineteen twelve? Drop your thoughts below.
In nineteen fifty-three, Calgarians lined up for days to buy City lots in a suburb first drawn before the First World War.
To see how the City ended up holding so much empty land, go back to the crash. As land sales fell, so did the City's tax collections.
The City was reluctant to take land when taxes went unpaid. It treated those unpaid taxes as assets.
In the end, it acquired by default a very large quantity of land which it did not want.
Most landowners, historian Max Foran writes, either sold at basement prices, or, more often than not, defaulted.
In nineteen nineteen, the tax arrears were announced publicly, and owners of Lake View Heights lots were on the list.
By the nineteen sixteen census, Calgary counted about fifty-six and a half thousand people. After that, it grew only modestly for decades.
So the map the boom had drawn sat waiting.

In Parkdale, a number of unsold lots appear to have been disposed of or forfeited under a tax recovery act used by the City. Aerial photos from nineteen twenty-four show a barren landscape with only a few scattered homes.
In Bowness, the land John Hextall planned in nineteen eleven sat vacant until after the Second World War, when a settlement for veterans was built.
In Killarney, most of the building came when soldiers returned from that war.
Highwood, which had reverted to the City for unpaid taxes, finally took shape after nineteen fifty-five.
And Spruce Cliff, first subdivided before the First World War, was subdivided again in nineteen fifty-three. Buyers lined up for days for one hundred and eighteen City lots.
Remember that five-hundred-dollar lot? It sat in a field that became Cambrian Heights, developed in nineteen fifty-five.
Drive through these communities today, and you are driving through a map first drawn in the boom.
